cls: Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID); active metabolite of fenbufen
quick: Apply 3% gel or foam (about 1 g, ~25-50 mg felbinac) to the affected area 2-4 times daily; max ~25 g gel/day
Avoid, especially in the third trimester (NSAID class effect on fetal circulation)
Limited data; topical systemic exposure is low but caution advised
Systemic absorption low; caution in significant renal impairment
Systemic absorption low; caution in hepatic impairment
No specific interaction with topical use
Local skin reaction; usual NSAID cautions if extensive/prolonged use
summary: Felbinac is a topical NSAID (the active metabolite of fenbufen, a biphenylacetic acid derivative) applied as a gel or cutaneous foam for the local symptomatic relief of pain and inflammation in soft-tissue injuries such as sprains, strains, and contusions, and in some regions for musculoskeletal/rheumatic pain. It inhibits cyclo-oxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis at the application site. Because absorption through intact skin is low, systemic NSAID adverse effects are uncommon, but the usual NSAID cautions apply. It is not FDA-approved; evidence/use derive from EMA/SmPC and BNF.
indications: Local symptomatic relief of pain and inflammation in soft-tissue injuries: sprains, strains, contusions, and sports injuries
Symptomatic relief of localized musculoskeletal and rheumatic pain (region/product specific)

dosage.r: Adult and adolescent (typically >=12-16 years per product)
dosage.d: Apply approximately 1 g of 3% gel or foam (delivering about 25-50 mg felbinac) to the affected area and rub in gently
dosage.n: Maximum about 25 g of gel per day; do not use longer than ~2 weeks without review
Use only as directed by product labeling/clinician

admin: Apply a thin layer to the intact skin over the painful or inflamed area and rub in gently
Wash hands after application (unless the hands are the site being treated)
Do not apply to broken skin, mucous membranes, eyes, or open wounds
Do not use under occlusive dressings unless advised; avoid excessive sun exposure of treated areas
moa: Felbinac is a biphenylacetic acid NSAID that inhibits cyclo-oxygenase enzymes, reducing the local synthesis of prostaglandins that mediate pain, inflammation, and swelling. Applied topically, it penetrates to underlying soft tissues to provide a local anti-inflammatory and analgesic effect while minimizing systemic prostaglandin inhibition.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to felbinac, fenbufen, aspirin, or other NSAIDs
History of asthma, urticaria, or allergic reactions precipitated by aspirin or other NSAIDs
Application to broken or diseased skin, mucous membranes, or eyes
relative: History of peptic ulcer or NSAID intolerance (with extensive/prolonged use)
Significant renal or hepatic impairment (with extensive use)
monitor: Standard NSAID precautions if applied over large areas or for prolonged periods

preg: Felbinac should be avoided during pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester, because NSAIDs as a class can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and may affect labor and fetal renal function. Use only if clearly necessary and not in late pregnancy.
lact: There are limited data on felbinac in breast milk. Systemic exposure after topical use is low; use with caution and avoid applying to the breast area while breastfeeding.
renal: Systemic absorption from topical felbinac is low, so renal effects are uncommon, but caution is advised in patients with significant renal impairment, particularly with extensive or prolonged application.
hepatic: Systemic absorption is low; caution is advised in patients with hepatic impairment if used over large areas or for prolonged periods.

major: No significant major interactions expected with normal topical use due to low systemic absorption
moderate: Other NSAIDs / aspirin (theoretical additive NSAID effect with extensive use)
minor: Photosensitizing agents (possible additive skin photosensitivity at the application site)
interactions.alcohol: No specific pharmacologic interaction with topical use
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory test interference at usual topical doses

common: Local skin reactions: erythema, irritation, itching, rash at the application site
rare: Systemic NSAID effects (gastrointestinal upset) with extensive or prolonged use
emergency: Severe allergic reaction / anaphylaxis (swelling, difficulty breathing)

monitoring: Local skin tolerability at the application site
Photosensitivity if treated skin is exposed to sunlight
Standard NSAID precautions if used over large areas or for an extended duration
counsel: Apply a thin layer to the painful area and rub in gently, up to the number of times directed
Wash your hands after applying unless you are treating your hands
Do not put it on broken skin, eyes, or mucous membranes
Stop and tell your doctor if you get a rash, severe irritation, or any wheezing or swelling
Protect treated skin from strong sunlight
Do not use for longer than the recommended period (usually about 2 weeks) without advice
pk: Local analgesic effect over hours of regular application
Low systemic plasma concentrations; tissue levels exceed plasma at the application site
Systemic exposure low; eliminated mainly as conjugates in urine
Store at room temperature; keep the cap closed; flammable foam preparations should be kept away from flame
pearls: NOTE: Felbinac is NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF (e.g., UK Traxam) rather than an FDA label
Felbinac is the active metabolite of the oral NSAID fenbufen, used directly as a topical agent
Topical delivery achieves high local tissue concentrations with low systemic exposure, limiting systemic NSAID toxicity
Cross-reactivity means it must be avoided in patients with aspirin/NSAID-induced asthma or urticaria
Useful for localized soft-tissue injury but should be combined with rest, ice, compression, and elevation for acute strains/sprains
missed: Felbinac is applied as needed on a regular daily schedule; if an application is missed, apply it when remembered and continue the usual routine. Do not apply extra to make up for a missed application.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely with topical use because of low systemic absorption. Accidental ingestion of the gel could cause NSAID-type gastrointestinal upset; manage supportively with general NSAID overdose measures (consider activated charcoal if a large amount is ingested recently, supportive care, and monitoring of renal and gastrointestinal status). There is no specific antidote.
